nameStory: The Pacific chorus frog gets its name from its Pacific Northwest homeland, where these little amphibians are famous for their loud, synchronized evening concerts. Male frogs gather in large groups during breeding season and call together in a chorus that can be heard from surprising distances, creating one of the most recognizable sounds of the western wetlands.
description: The Pacific chorus frog is a small, adaptable tree frog that's naturally found along the Pacific Coast from California to Alaska. These compact frogs are masterful color-changers, shifting between shades of green and brown over hours or weeks to match their surroundings. They're excellent climbers with sticky toe pads, though they spend time both in trees and on the ground near water.

idTips.label: Color/Pattern
idTips.description: Can change from bright green to chocolate brown over time, often with a dark stripe running through the eye like a bandit's mask

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Smooth, slightly moist skin that feels cool and clean to the touch, not warty or bumpy like a toad

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to sit comfortably on a quarter, rarely larger than your thumbnail

idTips.label: Call
idTips.description: High-pitched 'kreck-ek' or 'ribbit' sound, the classic frog call you hear in movies

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, prominent eyes that bulge outward, often with golden or bronze coloring

habitat: In New England, Pacific chorus frogs are extremely rare visitors, likely arriving as hitchhikers in plant shipments or as escaped pets. If found, they'd be near water sources like ponds, streams, or even temporary puddles, possibly in gardens or nurseries where western plants have been imported.

seasonality.spring: Any individuals in New England would likely be calling near temporary pools if they survive the winter, though this would be extraordinary.
seasonality.summer: Most active period if present, when they'd be easiest to spot near water sources or climbing on vegetation during warm, humid evenings.
seasonality.fall: Would be preparing for winter dormancy, becoming less active and harder to find as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Would likely not survive New England winters outdoors, as they're not adapted to our harsh cold and snow.

funFact: Pacific chorus frogs can live at elevations over 10,000 feet in their native range - higher than many ski resorts - making them one of the highest-dwelling frogs in North America!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with the native Spring Peeper, but Pacific chorus frogs have a dark eye stripe (peepers have an X on their back) and can change color dramatically, while peepers stay consistently tan to brown.
contextualKnowledge: With only 2 observations recorded in New England, seeing a Pacific chorus frog here would be like finding a celebrity in your backyard - they're western natives that have somehow made an incredible journey across the continent, likely with human help.
compareHints: Unlike its cousin the Spring Peeper, the Pacific chorus frog has the distinctive dark eye stripe and amazing color-changing ability. Spring Peepers keep their brown tones year-round and sport that characteristic X-shaped cross on their backs, while Pacific chorus frogs can shift from green to brown like tiny chameleons.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Spring peepers are the only Pseudacris chorus frog commonly found in New England, making them unique in their genus here.
